channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: [32] Valerian, chamomile, and lavender for insomnia and sleep disturbance: a narrative review of mechanisms, clinical efficacy, and safety.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic, clinical, and safety evidence for valerian, chamomile, and lavender in adults with insomnia disorder or sleep disturbance, prioritizing randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, and guidelines from a structured literature search.
FINDINGS: Valerian showed minimal and inconsistent effects on subjective sleep quality with no consistent impact on objective sleep latency or total sleep time; evidence quality was low. Chamomile reduced Sleep Quality scores in small, heterogeneous trials, while oral lavender oil (Silexan) appeared to improve disturbed sleep primarily by reducing anxiety in patients with anxiety disorders. Evidence varied by preparation, dose, route, and population.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak due to small samples, heterogeneity, and methodological limitations; no meta-analysis or formal risk-of-bias assessment was performed. Findings suggest no robust support for these botanicals as alternatives to first-line insomnia treatments. High-quality, adequately powered trials with objective outcomes and adverse-event monitoring are needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify recommending valerian, chamomile, or lavender as alternatives to guideline-based insomnia treatments; clinicians should discuss use with patients, acknowledging product variability and limited efficacy data.

item.title: [25] Rethinking opioid therapy in chronic pain: Role of neurobiology.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review (2015–2025) examines the neurobiological rationale for limiting long-term opioid therapy in chronic non-cancer pain and proposes a structured, multimodal, patient-centred alternative for primary care. It synthesizes systematic reviews, RCTs, and guidelines to argue that chronic pain is primarily a CNS-mediated threat response rather than persistent nociceptive input.
FINDINGS: The review cites level I evidence that long-term opioids provide at best modest benefit for chronic pain and level I evidence of harms (tolerance, dependence, opioid-induced hyperalgesia, OUD). Level II evidence frames pain as a CNS output modulated by threat appraisal. A multimodal framework (the “5 Ps”: pain education, physical activity, psychological strategies, pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic supports) is supported by level I–II evidence for improving function.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative synthesis, this paper is not designed to yield precise effect sizes or confidence intervals. Its strength lies in integrating diverse high-quality sources to challenge opioid-first paradigms. However, narrative reviews are susceptible to selection and confirmation bias. The clinical recommendations rest on mechanistic plausibility and aggregated evidence rather than head-to-head trials of the proposed framework versus usual care. External validity hinges on primary care settings where multimodal resources are available.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For patients with chronic pain, clinicians should prioritize non-opioid, function-focused strategies and reserve time-limited opioid trials for carefully selected cases with clear functional goals and close monitoring. Watch for escalating doses or paradoxical hyperalgesia as red flags.

item.title: [20] Psychological support for women following perinatal loss: a systematic review of clinical practice guidance.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) to identify and appraise psychological recommendations for supporting women’s mental health after perinatal loss (pregnancy or early postnatal death). It assessed the quality of existing guidance and synthesized recommendations to highlight gaps in psychological care.
FINDINGS: Sixteen guidelines were included; ten rated “excellent,” four “good,” and two “average” in methodological quality. Recommendations covered psychological assessment, interventions, psychosocial support, service provision, and systemic factors, but consistency and specificity varied widely. Few guidelines provided clear guidance on follow-up or long-term psychological assessment.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited by heterogeneous and sometimes vague recommendations, with only moderate methodological quality in many guidelines. The lack of standardized, evidence-based follow-up protocols risks under-detection of mental health difficulties in grieving women. While the review identifies areas for improvement, it does not provide effect sizes or direct clinical outcomes, making it difficult to assess clinical impact.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current guidelines offer fragmented psychological support after perinatal loss. Clinicians should be aware of these gaps and consider individualized, trauma-informed follow-up, while advocating for the development of standardized, evidence-based CPGs to improve care quality.

item.title: [19] Psychiatrists' Prescribing Choice Determinants for Brexpiprazole and Other Antipsychotics in Patients With Schizophrenia: Results From a National Congress-Based Survey in Argentina.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional, convenience survey examined Argentine psychiatrists' self-reported antipsychotic prescribing patterns for schizophrenia, with a focus on awareness and use of brexpiprazole, clozapine, and long-acting injectable antipsychotics (LAIs). The study aimed to identify factors influencing prescribing choices in routine practice.
FINDINGS: Among 371 psychiatrists (60.1% female, mean age 38.7 years), second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs) were prescribed by 80.3% of respondents. Clozapine was used in 12.8% of patients, LAIs in 11.6%, while brexpiprazole was prescribed by only 29.1% of respondents (3.9% of total prescriptions), with limited availability, cost, and lack of experience cited as barriers. Factors most strongly associated with clozapine and LAI prescribing included higher proportions of treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS) patients and greater clinical exposure to schizophrenia. Key determinants for antipsychotic selection were positive symptom efficacy (90.0%), tolerability (70.0%), negative symptom efficacy (64.7%), and lower cardiometabolic risk (54.9%).
INTERPRETATION: This study provides exploratory, hypothesis-generating data on prescribing patterns in Argentina, but its cross-sectional design and reliance on self-reported data limit causal inference. The sample, drawn from a national congress, may not represent all psychiatrists, particularly those in non-academic or rural settings. The low uptake of brexpiprazole and identified barriers suggest practical constraints (e.g., cost, availability) rather than clinical preference. The findings highlight perceived challenges in schizophrenia treatment but cannot determine effectiveness or optimal prescribing strategies.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The study suggests that brexpiprazole remains underutilized in Argentina due to systemic barriers rather than clinical inefficacy. Clinicians should be aware of these constraints when considering newer SGAs. However, the lack of comparative effectiveness data means no firm treatment recommendations can be made based on this survey alone.

item.title: [18] Reducing re-hospitalization in schizophrenia: real-world comparison of first- vs. second-generation long-acting injectable antipsychotics.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study compared first-generation (FGA) versus second-generation (SGA) long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotics in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSDs) to assess differences in reducing hospitalizations, relapses, and suicide attempts. This mirror-image, retrospective cohort study evaluated 133 patients over three years after switching from oral antipsychotics to LAIs.
FINDINGS: Hospital admissions decreased from 53.4% to 6.0% after LAI initiation, and the average hospitalization duration dropped from 14.26 days (±29.1) to 1.35 days (±8.09). Both FGA-LAIs and SGA-LAIs reduced hospitalizations, relapses, and suicide attempts, but no statistically significant differences were found between the two groups.
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates a strong association between LAI initiation and reduced hospitalizations and relapses, but the mirror-image design (pre-post comparison without a concurrent control group) limits causal inference. Residual confounding and lack of randomization weaken internal validity, and the predominantly male, middle-aged, Caucasian sample limits generalizability. The lack of difference between FGA- and SGA-LAIs suggests no clear superiority of one class over the other in this cohort.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: LAIs appear effective in reducing rehospitalizations in SSD, but the choice between FGA- and SGA-LAIs should remain individualized based on tolerability, patient preference, and clinical judgment rather than assumed superiority of one class.

item.title: [16] Psychotropic drug-induced lipid disturbances: a genome-wide association study in a Swiss psychiatric cohort.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This genome-wide association study (GWAS) in a Swiss psychiatric cohort (PsyMetab, n=829) investigated genetic variants influencing lipid changes induced by psychotropic drugs (e.g., antipsychotics, lithium, mirtazapine) over up to one year of treatment. The study aimed to identify genetic contributors to dyslipidemia in psychiatric patients, a clinically relevant issue given the metabolic side effects of these medications.
FINDINGS: Seven loci reached genome-wide significance (P < 5 × 10⁻⁸) for associations with treatment-induced lipid changes. Three variants were linked to total cholesterol changes (e.g., rs17313064 with aripiprazole/quetiapine), two to HDL-cholesterol changes (e.g., rs12097296 with lithium/mirtazapine), one to triglycerides with risperidone (rs10260518), and one to triglycerides across any drug (rs56286230). Sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of rs10933971’s effect on HDL-cholesterol across varying timeframes.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s strengths include its longitudinal design and focus on drug-specific genetic effects, but limitations include the lack of classical replication and potential confounding by heterogeneous drug exposures. The findings suggest plausible genetic targets (e.g., lipid-regulating genes) but require validation in independent cohorts. The clinical significance is unclear, as effect sizes and allele frequencies were not reported, and the study does not yet translate to actionable pharmacogenomic guidelines.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current practice remains unchanged; this is preliminary evidence for genetic predictors of psychotropic-induced dyslipidemia. Clinicians should continue monitoring metabolic parameters in patients on these drugs while awaiting further validation and clinical utility studies.

item.title: [14] Treatment response prediction in major neurocognitive disorder with depression using the scalp-to-cortex distance of TMS targets: implications for personalized dose estimation.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study asks whether scalp-to-cortex distance (SCD) of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) targets can predict antidepressant response in elderly patients with major neurocognitive disorder and depression, using data from a secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial (RCT) with 55 participants.
FINDINGS: Responders to active 10 Hz rTMS had a greater SCD at left M1, a lower SCD_DLPFC/M1 ratio, and higher SCD-modified output difference (SCD-MOOD) than nonresponders. Logistic regression showed associations between remission and SCD of left M1 (p = 0.038) and SCD-MOOD (p = 0.042). A classification model using SCD metrics achieved 92.5% accuracy at week 3 and 86.2% at week 12. The model showed strong specificity for distinguishing active from sham stimulation.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and based on a small secondary analysis of an RCT with no correction for multiple comparisons. The high accuracy metrics may reflect overfitting in a small sample (n=55) and require external validation. The clinical utility of SCD-based prediction remains uncertain until replicated in larger, adequately powered studies with longer follow-up and blinding integrity checks.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not justify changing routine practice. SCD metrics may one day guide personalized TMS dosing, but further validation is needed before considering adoption in clinical settings.

item.title: [12] Microdosing Approach for Switching From Methadone to Buprenorphine in Opioid Disorder: A French Case Series.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether a 14-day microdosing protocol can facilitate switching from methadone to buprenorphine in patients with opioid use disorder in routine French outpatient settings, addressing the challenge of withdrawal during conventional induction. This case series reports on 10 patients treated at two specialist addiction centers in Lyon, France.
FINDINGS: Of 10 patients (8 men, 2 women), 6 (60%) successfully completed the transition using the microdosing protocol, including five outpatients. Withdrawal symptoms were absent or mild in successful transfers. Two patients discontinued due to withdrawal symptoms, and two were lost to follow-up. No severe adverse events were reported.
INTERPRETATION: This is a small, retrospective case series with no control group, limiting causal inference and generalizability. The 60% completion rate and absence of severe adverse events suggest feasibility, but selection bias, lack of standardized withdrawal assessment, and short follow-up (no duration specified) weaken internal validity. Larger prospective studies with standardized outcomes are needed to confirm efficacy, safety, and cost-effectiveness.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Microdosing may offer an outpatient alternative for methadone-to-buprenorphine transfer, potentially reducing hospitalization needs, but current evidence is preliminary. Clinicians should proceed cautiously, monitor for withdrawal, and consider this approach only within structured protocols pending further evidence.

item.title: [10] The effects of psychoeducation-supported breathing and relaxation exercises on Post-Traumatic stress symptoms and sleep quality in earthquake survivors.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study tested whether a brief, group-based psychoeducation-supported breathing and relaxation program could reduce post-traumatic stress symptoms and improve sleep quality in adults living in temporary shelters after the February 2023 earthquakes in Malatya, Türkiye. It used a randomized controlled pre–post design.
FINDINGS: Ninety adults were randomized (42 intervention, 42 control); 84 completed the trial. After six sessions, the intervention group’s PTSD-SS score fell by 5.45 points versus control (p < .05), and PSQI score fell by 3.88 points (p < .05), indicating reduced PTSD symptoms and better sleep.
INTERPRETATION: The RCT shows a statistically significant benefit, but the clinical magnitude is modest and the follow-up was only post-treatment with no longer-term data. The unblinded self-report outcomes and lack of an active comparator raise risk of bias. Funding sources and effect sizes with confidence intervals were not reported, limiting certainty.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The program may offer a low-cost, scalable adjunct to post-disaster care, but current evidence does not yet justify replacing standard trauma-focused therapies; further blinded trials with longer follow-up are needed.

item.title: [10] Real-World Data in Economic Evaluations of Schizophrenia: A Systematic Review of Roles, Applications and Methodological Gaps.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review (PROSPERO-registered, PRISMA-guided) examined how real-world data (RWD) have been incorporated into economic evaluations of schizophrenia (2015–2025), focusing on roles, methodological quality and reporting transparency. The 30 included studies comprised 15 model-based, 12 observational and three trial-based evaluations.
FINDINGS: Across the 30 studies, RWD were most often used to populate clinical event rates, healthcare utilisation and costs, but rarely informed health utilities or broader societal outcomes. In model-based analyses, RWD mainly entered as individual parameters rather than shaping model structure or full care pathways. Observational studies used patient-level RWD directly, yet several had small samples (n<200) and few reported formal confounding adjustment. Trial-based evaluations primarily supplemented resource-use and cost data with RWD. Reporting completeness (CHEERS 2022) and EHR suitability (ISPOR SUITABILITY) were frequently inadequate, hampering assessment of data quality and analytical credibility.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is heterogeneous and methodologically limited. Strengths include the systematic search and use of established reporting/checklist tools; weaknesses include incomplete reporting, small observational samples, and limited use of RWD to inform model structure or long-term pathways. The current pattern of RWD use may not fully address decision-makers’ needs for long-term, routine-practice evidence. Until methodological gaps are addressed, readers should view these findings as preliminary and context-specific rather than definitive.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For now, RWD can complement—but not replace—traditional evidence sources in schizophrenia economic evaluations. Clinicians should be cautious when interpreting cost-effectiveness models that rely heavily on sparse or poorly validated RWD, and advocate for better reporting and methodological standards in future studies.

item.title: [7] The need for translational research to advance the understanding of substance use disorders.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review argues that translational research is needed to move from basic neuroscience to clinical treatments in substance use disorders (SUDs), highlighting the gap between promising preclinical findings and the paucity of approved medications.
FINDINGS: Preclinical models (e.g., operant self-administration) now capture DSM-5 addiction criteria in animals, and rodent fMRI is proposed to align animal and human neuroimaging. Despite these advances, few new medications have reached the clinic, underscoring a translational bottleneck.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is conceptual rather than quantitative; the paper identifies a clear translational gap and suggests methodological improvements (predictive validity, biomarker alignment) but does not provide effect sizes, p-values, or head-to-head comparisons. Strengths include breadth of cited models and explicit acknowledgment of current limitations; weaknesses include lack of systematic synthesis and absence of quantitative outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For now, this review changes nothing at the bedside; it serves as a call to strengthen translational pipelines and prioritize biomarker-driven trials rather than altering immediate practice.

item.title: [6] Cell-Type-Specific Cell-Free DNA methylation profiling of central nervous system injury and inflammatory cell turnover in schizophrenia.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) with cell-type-specific methylation patterns could distinguish schizophrenia-spectrum disorders from healthy controls and other psychiatric disorders, aiming to clarify immune and neuronal contributions to schizophrenia pathophysiology. It was a cross-sectional and longitudinal cohort study including 165 patients with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders, 52 with other psychiatric disorders, and 68 healthy controls.
FINDINGS: Patients with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders had higher total cfDNA concentrations than controls (p = 0.0006). Methylation analysis showed increased neuronal (p < 0.0001) and astrocyte-derived cfDNA (p = 0.015), alongside elevated innate and adaptive immune cfDNA (neutrophils, monocytes, B and T cells; p < 0.0001), while regulatory T cell cfDNA was unchanged (p > 0.99). ROC analysis discriminated schizophrenia from controls with an AUC of 0.76 and from other psychiatric disorders with an AUC of 0.62. In a longitudinal subset (n = 39), total and immune-derived cfDNA declined over three weeks, but brain-derived cfDNA remained elevated.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides preliminary evidence of elevated brain and immune cfDNA in schizophrenia, suggesting ongoing neuronal injury and immune activation. The longitudinal data indicate partial normalization of immune markers but persistent brain injury signals. However, the modest AUC values and lack of blinding or adjustment for multiple comparisons limit diagnostic utility. The sample is hospital-based, so results may not generalize to community settings. The findings are biologically plausible but require replication in larger, diverse cohorts with longer follow-up and clinical correlation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support using cfDNA methylation profiling as a diagnostic or monitoring tool in routine psychiatric care. The study highlights potential pathophysiological mechanisms but remains exploratory; further validation is needed before any clinical application.

item.title: [6] Multi-omics integration identifies COQ8A in excitatory neurons as a protective gene in major depressive disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This translational study used multi-omics integration (eQTL, GWAS, and single-nucleus RNA-seq) to identify cell-specific genes implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD) pathogenesis, focusing on excitatory neurons and oligodendrocytes.
FINDINGS: The study identified 26 candidate genes, with COQ8A significantly downregulated in excitatory neurons and LATS1 upregulated in oligodendrocytes in MDD patients. Chronic social defeat stress models in mice confirmed COQ8A downregulation in prefrontal cortex excitatory neurons. Functional analyses linked COQ8A downregulation to impaired energy metabolism, mitochondrial function, and protein synthesis. Molecular docking suggested high-affinity binding of eight antidepressants (including escitalopram and paroxetine) to COQ8A.
INTERPRETATION: This is a hypothesis-generating, multi-omics study with no direct clinical intervention. While the integration of genetic, transcriptomic, and functional data strengthens biological plausibility, causal relationships remain unproven. The findings are preliminary and require validation in larger, clinically diverse cohorts. The clinical relevance of COQ8A as a therapeutic target is speculative until functional or interventional studies confirm benefit.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No immediate change in practice is warranted. COQ8A may represent a future research target for precision psychiatry, but current evidence is insufficient to guide treatment decisions or biomarker development.

item.title: [24] Does timing matter-meta-analysis and systematic review of digital cognitive behavioral therapy in the perinatal period.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The review asks whether the timing of digital cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) in the perinatal period—during pregnancy, after childbirth, or across both periods—affects its effectiveness for reducing depressive symptoms. Sixteen randomized controlled trials (n=7577) were synthesized to compare outcomes by delivery window.
FINDINGS: Across all trials, digital CBT produced a modest but statistically significant reduction in depressive symptoms versus control (pooled mean difference −2.03, 95 % CI −2.73 to −1.34). Meta-regression suggested postpartum delivery may be more effective than antenatal delivery (b = −1.99, 95 % CI −3.90 to −0.08, p = 0.04), but this contrast became marginally non-significant (p = 0.051) when one high-risk-of-bias study was excluded.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate-sized and heterogeneous; the overall effect is small and likely to vary by population and platform. The apparent timing advantage is fragile and sensitive to risk-of-bias adjustments, so it should be treated as preliminary rather than definitive. Larger, well-controlled RCTs with standardized timing strata are needed to confirm any differential benefit.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Digital CBT remains a viable, scalable option for perinatal depression, but current data do not justify choosing postpartum over antenatal delivery based on efficacy alone; implementation should be guided by patient preference, access, and clinical need rather than assumed timing superiority.

item.title: [17] A pilot randomized controlled trial of a transdiagnostic multidomain lifestyle intervention for psychiatric outpatients: feasibility, acceptability and preliminary effectiveness for improving recovery.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This pilot RCT (n=46) tested a 12-week transdiagnostic multidomain lifestyle intervention (group sessions + follow-ups) versus treatment-as-usual in psychiatric outpatients, assessing feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary recovery outcomes.
FINDINGS: Recruitment and retention were acceptable (83% retention; 71% session attendance; 13% dropout). Participants rated the intervention 7.4/10, with no serious risks reported. Exploratory analyses showed positive trends across recovery domains, particularly societal and personal recovery at follow-up, but effect estimates were imprecise (95% CIs included zero).
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates feasibility and high acceptability in a heterogeneous outpatient sample, with no major safety concerns. However, as a small pilot RCT, it is underpowered for definitive effectiveness conclusions; the exploratory positive trends require confirmation in a fully powered trial with adequate sample size and longer follow-up.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence supports the feasibility of implementing such interventions in routine care, but does not yet justify routine adoption for improving recovery outcomes; further trials are needed to determine clinical efficacy and cost-effectiveness.

item.title: [12] Cognitive Impairment in Bipolar Disorder: A Clinician-focused Narrative Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This clinician-focused narrative review synthesizes recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses to summarize cognitive impairment in bipolar disorder (BD), a clinically relevant but under-evaluated feature that may impact functional recovery and illness progression across all mood states.
FINDINGS: Cognitive deficits—particularly in verbal memory and executive functioning—affect over half of patients with BD, including during remission. These deficits are present from the first episode of mania, persist across illness stages, and are more pronounced in older patients and those with comorbidities. Current pro-cognitive interventions (pharmacological and non-pharmacological) show preliminary or inconsistent evidence, and routine screening is recommended alongside management of modifiable contributors.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this study synthesizes existing evidence without new primary data, limiting causal inference and generalizability. The findings highlight the prevalence and heterogeneity of cognitive impairment in BD but rely on aggregated data from prior systematic reviews/meta-analyses, which may vary in quality and methodology. The clinical significance of the reported deficits is supported by links to functional outcomes, though the lack of robust intervention trials leaves uncertainty about effective management strategies.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should consider routine screening for cognitive impairment in BD, especially in older or comorbid patients, and address modifiable factors (e.g., lifestyle, treatment side effects). However, evidence for targeted pro-cognitive treatments remains insufficient to recommend specific interventions beyond standard care.

item.title: [12] Orexin receptor antagonists for sleep disturbance in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and autism spectrum disorder: a systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The review asks whether orexin receptor antagonists (ORAs) improve sleep in patients with ADHD or ASD, where melatonin’s limitations leave a therapeutic gap. It synthesises all published and registered human data up to Sept 2023 using PRISMA methods, but Embase and PsycINFO were not searched.
FINDINGS: Eight reports (41 exposed individuals: 25 ADHD, 16 ASD) were identified. In a single open-label 50 mg daridorexant study in 24 adults with ADHD, median ISI fell from 16 to 8 and actigraphic total sleep time increased by ≈24 min; 62.5 % met response criteria. No controlled, diagnosis-specific trials exist; paediatric data are absent. ASD evidence consists of small, confounded case reports and one null comparison. Two registered trials are underway, one completed but without published stratified results.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is extremely thin (n=41, no RCTs, high risk of bias) and pooling was impossible. The observed sleep improvements in ADHD are statistically significant but derive from a single open-label study; cognitive and attention claims are fragile and post-hoc. GRADE certainty is very low; causal inference is unwarranted. The mechanistic rationale remains untested in controlled trials.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine use of ORAs for sleep in ADHD/ASD cannot be recommended. Any off-label trial should be reserved for specialist settings with prospective outcome tracking and shared decision-making about uncertain benefits and unknown long-term risks.

item.title: [11] Cognitive behavioral therapy and physical activity: a viewpoint on combined approaches for young people at clinical high risk for psychosis or with first-episode psychosis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative viewpoint examines whether combining cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) with physical activity (PA) could address unmet needs in young people at clinical high risk for psychosis or with first-episode psychosis, where CBT alone has limited impact on negative symptoms, cognition, and physical health deterioration.
FINDINGS: The paper synthesizes existing trials from other psychiatric and medical populations suggesting that PA improves negative symptoms, cognition, and cardiometabolic health—areas where CBT for psychosis is less effective. It proposes a continuum of integration models from parallel delivery to fully integrated movement-based therapy, but notes that no randomized controlled trial (RCT) has yet tested a fully integrated PA-augmented CBT in early psychosis.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative viewpoint, this study offers theoretical and mechanistic support for combining CBT and PA but lacks direct empirical evidence in the target population. The strength of evidence is low due to the absence of RCTs and reliance on cross-disorder synthesis. The proposed integration models are plausible but untested, and the clinical benefit remains uncertain until factorial or optimization trials are conducted.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current practice should not yet adopt integrated CBT-PA as standard care for early psychosis. Clinicians may consider adjunctive PA as part of general health promotion, but formal integration into CBT should await trial evidence. Watch for emerging RCTs testing combined models before changing treatment protocols.

item.title: [8] Nocebo-induced cardiopulmonary symptoms following sertraline initiation mimicking acute cardiac pathology: a case report.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: A single case report describes acute cardiopulmonary symptoms mimicking cardiac pathology shortly after starting sertraline in a 32-year-old woman with moderate major depressive disorder, highlighting the potential role of nocebo effects in early SSRI initiation.
FINDINGS: Within 48 hours of sertraline initiation, the patient experienced palpitations, dyspnea, dizziness, and chest tightness, prompting emergency evaluation. Investigations revealed sinus tachycardia, normal cardiac biomarkers, borderline left ventricular ejection fraction (51%) on echocardiography, and no acute intracranial pathology on MRI. Symptoms resolved with reassurance, and sertraline was successfully reintroduced at a lower dose after expectation-targeted counseling, with normalized LVEF (58%) and improved depressive symptoms (Hamilton Depression Rating Scale-17 from 21 to 10) at five-week follow-up.
INTERPRETATION: As a case report, the evidence is anecdotal with no control group, making causality uncertain and generalizability limited. The temporal association with sertraline initiation, symptom resolution with reassurance, and absence of recurrence upon rechallenge suggest a probable nocebo mechanism, but early SSRI-related adverse effects cannot be entirely excluded. The study lacks quantitative effect sizes or statistical analysis, relying on clinical observation and subjective reporting.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This case underscores the importance of recognizing nocebo effects in patients with pre-treatment exposure to negative information about antidepressants, which may lead to unnecessary investigations and discontinuation. Clinicians should proactively address patient expectations through psychoeducation and gradual dose titration to improve adherence and reduce diagnostic uncertainty.

item.title: [7] Reducing Caregiver Depression in Schizophrenia: A Retrospective Quasi-Experimental Study of a CBT-Based Psychoeducational Program Using a Waiting-Period Control.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study asks whether a CBT-based multifamily psychoeducational program (Profamille) reduces depressive symptoms among caregivers of people with schizophrenia, using a retrospective quasi-experimental design with a waiting-period control. The population was French caregivers enrolled in Profamille V3.2 between 2011–2019.
FINDINGS: In 1,117 active participants versus 1,116 pseudo-controls, 29% of initially depressed caregivers (CES-D >16) remitted post-intervention vs 8% in controls (absolute difference 21%). Among those with subclinical depression, 53% remitted vs 25% in controls (absolute difference 28%). Non-depressed caregivers remained stable, with a trend toward preventive benefit. Missing data were 12.3%.
INTERPRETATION: The large sample and consistent subgroup effects strengthen confidence, but the retrospective, non-randomised design and reliance on archival data introduce selection and attrition biases. There was no blinding, and clinical representativeness depends on French service uptake. The absolute risk reductions are clinically meaningful, yet causal inference is limited by design.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Profamille may meaningfully reduce depressive symptoms in schizophrenia caregivers; however, confirmatory RCTs are needed before practice change. Clinicians should consider offering psychoeducation while monitoring for selection and attrition biases in routine care.

item.title: [7] Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement and Emergency Department Visits in Opioid Use: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement (MORE) reduces emergency department (ED) visits and associated costs among veterans receiving long-term opioid therapy (LTOT) for chronic pain, using secondary data from a single-blind randomized clinical trial (RCT).
FINDINGS: In the 185 veterans (mean age 57.5 years, 16.8% women) randomized to MORE or supportive psychotherapy, MORE was associated with fewer ED visits during months 9–12 (0.54 vs 0.72 visits per participant; IRR 0.29, 95% CI 0.13–0.65, P = .01) but not earlier. PAMH-related ED visits were also reduced (IRR 0.22, 95% CI 0.07–0.74, P = .04). ED-associated costs were lower with MORE ($769.83 vs $1043.33).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests MORE may reduce long-term ED utilization and costs, but effects emerged only after 9–12 months, raising questions about durability and mechanisms. The single-blind design and secondary analysis limit causal inference; unmeasured confounders and reliance on EHR data are key weaknesses. The small effect size and delayed onset warrant cautious interpretation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: MORE could be considered for veterans on LTOT with chronic pain to potentially reduce long-term ED use, but evidence is preliminary and not yet sufficient to change routine practice without further validation.

item.title: [7] Exploring Indigenous Methodologies to Inform Guideline Development: A Scoping Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This scoping review examined Indigenous research methodologies to inform the development of Indigenous-led guidelines for addressing disproportionately high suicide rates among Indigenous Peoples in Canada, particularly youth. The review aimed to identify methodologies that could guide culturally appropriate guideline creation.
FINDINGS: Twenty-two articles were included after systematic searches of academic and grey literature. Three Indigenous methodologies were identified: Storytelling, Etuaptmumk (Two-Eyed Seeing), and Decolonization and Indigenization. The review emphasizes the necessity of integrating these methodologies to ensure Indigenous leadership and co-creation in guideline development to address suicide disparities.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and descriptive, based on a scoping review rather than a systematic synthesis of clinical outcomes. Strengths include the inclusion of Indigenous expert review and a focus on culturally grounded approaches. However, the lack of quantitative outcomes or direct comparisons limits conclusions about effectiveness. The findings highlight the importance of methodological frameworks but do not yet provide actionable clinical guidance.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This review underscores the need for Indigenous-led, culturally informed approaches in guideline development but does not yet offer specific clinical recommendations. Clinicians should remain aware of the importance of cultural context in mental health care for Indigenous populations while awaiting further evidence.

item.title: [7] Longitudinal impact of physical activity on physical and psychological outcomes and healthcare costs in severe mental disorders: a 15-month quasi-experimental community study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This 15-month quasi-experimental community study in adults with severe mental disorders (SMD: schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder) examined whether engagement in a structured physical activity (PA) programme improved physical and psychological outcomes and reduced healthcare costs compared with treatment as usual.
FINDINGS: Of 156 participants (78 PA, 78 control), the PA group showed greater improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness, body composition (including visceral adiposity), and mental well-being (WEMWBS) at 15 months (p < .001). Quality of life (WHOQOL-BREF) gains and behavioural improvements were also higher in the PA group. Exploratory cost analysis suggested lower direct healthcare expenditures in the PA group, mainly due to reduced psychiatric hospitalisations and medication costs.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s quasi-experimental design (non-randomised, matched groups) and baseline differences in fitness/behavioural variables limit causal inference. While the magnitude of physical and psychological improvements appears clinically meaningful, cost findings are preliminary and require confirmatory economic evaluation. The real-world setting enhances external validity, but unmeasured confounders (e.g., lifestyle changes, social support) may bias results.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Structured PA may be a beneficial adjunct in community SMD care, potentially improving physical health, well-being, and reducing hospitalisation risk. However, clinicians should await randomised trials before prioritising PA programmes over established treatments, and interpret cost savings cautiously.

item.title: [7] A peer-group programme for people with severe mental illness to reduce risk of cardiometabolic disease (PEGASUS): protocol for a feasibility study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: People with severe mental illness (SMI) have a 15–20-year shorter life expectancy, largely due to a 50 % higher risk of cardiometabolic disease. PEGASUS is a single-arm, mixed-methods feasibility study across three NHS trusts in England, co-designed with lived experience, to test a peer-led group intervention aimed at reducing cardiometabolic risk in adults aged 18–75 with SMI and elevated CVD risk.
FINDINGS: The study will recruit participants with SMI and enhanced CVD risk into ten fortnightly group sessions led by a peer support worker and a healthcare professional, plus four one-to-one sessions and a booster. Data collection includes biometrics, accelerometry, questionnaires, and qualitative interviews at baseline, 3 and 6 months. Feasibility and acceptability of each measure will be assessed. Planned analyses include STATA for quantitative data and NVivo for rapid framework analysis of qualitative data.
INTERPRETATION: As a single-arm feasibility study without a control group, internal validity is limited and no causal inferences can be drawn. The focus is on acceptability, recruitment, retention, and data completeness to inform a future RCT. External validity will depend on the representativeness of the NHS trust settings and the willingness of participants with SMI to engage in group-based interventions. The absence of effect size estimates or comparative data precludes assessment of clinical significance at this stage.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This protocol signals a potentially scalable, peer-led approach to address a major cause of premature mortality in SMI, but no practice change is warranted until efficacy is demonstrated in a randomised trial. Clinicians should await the feasibility outcomes and subsequent RCT results before considering integration into routine care.

item.title: [6] Artificial intelligence-assisted screening of major depressive disorder using routine laboratory tests across multicenter cohorts.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study tests whether an AI model (MD3S) can screen for major depressive disorder (MDD) using routine laboratory and clinical data in large real-world cohorts. The clinical question is whether scalable, non-symptom-based screening is feasible; the design is a retrospective multicenter evaluation with internal and two external validation cohorts.
FINDINGS: In the UK Biobank internal validation (n≈180 000), MD3S achieved an accuracy of 86.57% (95% CI not reported) for distinguishing MDD from non-MDD. Performance remained robust in two independent external hospital cohorts, outperforming conventional machine learning and deep learning baselines and showing high computational efficiency.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary but promising. Strengths include large sample size, multicenter validation, and comparison against standard AI approaches. Key limitations are the retrospective design, lack of reported sensitivity/specificity or confidence intervals, and uncertain clinical applicability because the cohorts consist of individuals who already had documented MDD diagnoses (i.e., the model is trained to detect documented cases, not incident or undiagnosed MDD). External validity to routine psychiatric care is uncertain because laboratory panels may differ across settings and the model’s performance in real-time screening is untested.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, this AI tool cannot replace validated symptom-based assessments for diagnosing MDD. It may eventually support large-scale screening if prospective studies demonstrate clinically meaningful sensitivity/specificity and safety in undiagnosed populations.

item.title: [14] Is psychomotor retardation associated with treatment response in adults with depression? A secondary analysis of nine randomized controlled trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study investigated whether psychomotor retardation (PMR) in adults with unipolar depression predicts poorer treatment response across nine randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of pharmacological, psychological, and exercise-based interventions in primary care. The clinical question was whether PMR, a marker of greater illness severity, is associated with worse outcomes after adjusting for confounders.
FINDINGS: Among 4,290 participants (64.2% reporting PMR), PMR was linked to higher depression severity at 3–4 months (pooled z-score = 0.184, 95% CI [0.059, 0.309], p = 0.004, I² = 68.7%) and lower remission odds (pooled OR = 0.737, 95% CI [0.577, 0.941], p = 0.015, I² = 57.7%) after adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity, marital status, employment, and treatment allocation. Effects persisted after adjusting for core depressive symptoms but not after full baseline severity adjustment.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests PMR may signal poorer prognosis, but its prognostic value may largely reflect underlying depression severity rather than being an independent predictor. The high heterogeneity (I² > 50%) and reliance on self-reported PMR limit precision. The lack of blinding in PMR assessment and reliance on aggregated RCT data further constrain causal inference.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: PMR could serve as a simple clinical marker to flag patients at risk of poorer response, prompting closer monitoring or tailored interventions, though its incremental prognostic value beyond standard severity measures appears limited.

item.title: [10] Exploring Post-Traumatic Growth in Early Intervention Services for Psychosis: A Systematic Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review (PROSPERO-registered, PRISMA-guided) asked how post-traumatic growth (PTG) is conceptualised and reported among people receiving early intervention services (EIS) for first-episode psychosis, and which service features may foster such growth. Fourteen heterogeneous studies (2007–2023) from mainly high-income EIS settings were synthesised narratively.
FINDINGS: Across qualitative, quantitative and mixed-methods designs, reported growth centred on relational, identity and existential domains; less often on community contribution or “giving back.” Quantitative work largely relied on retrospective self-report (e.g., Posttraumatic Growth Inventory). EIS appeared to enable growth through validating relationships, recovery-oriented care, social re-engagement and meaning-supporting environments, but growth co-existed with ongoing trauma symptoms, coercive care, stigma and medication ambivalence. Methodological limitations included scarce longitudinal data, few behavioural indicators and incomplete integration of qualitative and quantitative findings.
INTERPRETATION: Confidence in the evidence is moderate-to-low due to methodological heterogeneity, retrospective designs and limited longitudinal follow-up. The overlap between PTG constructs and personal recovery suggests that growth may be better understood as part of broader recovery processes rather than a distinct outcome. The enabling role of EIS is plausible but not yet proven causally. Future research should incorporate longitudinal and mixed-methods designs, diversify assessment beyond PTG scales and examine behavioural and contextual indicators.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Trauma-informed, growth-supportive EIS practice—emphasising relational safety, collaborative meaning-making and realistic optimism—can be integrated now, while avoiding prescriptive expectations of growth and acknowledging ongoing distress. Watch for co-existing trauma symptoms and coercive experiences that may complicate recovery narratives.

item.title: [10] Consistent Across Studies, Divergent Across Outcomes: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis of Animal-Assisted Interventions for Autism Spectrum Disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This three-level meta-analysis examined whether animal-assisted interventions (AAI) improve behavioral outcomes in autistic children and adolescents, synthesizing controlled trials to clarify efficacy and moderators. The study addressed inconsistent findings across outcomes and assessed evidence certainty using GRADE.
FINDINGS: Seventeen studies (159 effect sizes; 677 unique participants) were included. The overall effect was small but statistically significant (Hedges’ g = 0.275, 95% CI [0.153, 0.397], p < .001), with low heterogeneity (I²_Level 2 = 32.2%, I²_Level 3 = 0%). Effects were strongest for communication (g = 0.597) and sensory outcomes (g = 0.590), and moderate for social functioning (g = 0.337). No moderators explained variation in effect sizes. Publication bias was not detected, but GRADE assessment rated the evidence as low certainty due to risk of bias and imprecision.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests AAI may yield small improvements in behavioral outcomes, particularly in social communication and sensory domains, but the overall certainty is low. The lack of moderator effects and low heterogeneity suggest consistency across studies, though most interventions were equestrian-based, limiting generalizability. The small effect size and low GRADE rating mean these findings should be interpreted cautiously; larger, high-quality RCTs are needed to confirm efficacy and explore long-term outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence supports a cautious, adjunctive role for AAI in autism care, particularly for social and sensory goals, but should not replace established interventions. Clinicians should consider patient preferences and monitor outcomes closely, given the low certainty of evidence.

item.title: [9] A systematic review of substance use disorder methylome-wide association studies in postmortem human brain.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined methylome-wide association studies (MWAS) of substance use disorders (SUDs) in postmortem human brain tissue to identify epigenetic (DNA methylation) patterns linked to SUDs across different substances (alcohol, opioids, cocaine, nicotine, methamphetamine, and illicit drugs). The review synthesized findings from 20 studies to assess shared and substance-specific epigenetic signals.
FINDINGS: The studies analyzed varied in brain regions, methylation platforms, and sample characteristics, with most focusing on methylation at cytosines followed by guanine (mCGs). Despite methodological heterogeneity and limited overlap within individual substances, consistent biological themes emerged, including differential methylation in genes related to neurodevelopment, inflammatory response, signaling, and transcriptional regulation. Cross-substance comparisons identified 525 genes implicated across at least two substances, suggesting shared methylomic signals. Exploratory drug repurposing analyses highlighted a small number of existing compounds with potential relevance for treating polysubstance use.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and heterogeneous, with significant methodological variability and limited sample sizes. The lack of functional validation and cell-type specificity limits the strength of conclusions. While shared biological themes and cross-substance gene overlaps suggest potential common neurobiological pathways, the translational potential remains uncertain. The review highlights the promise of MWAS in SUD research but underscores the need for larger, more diverse cohorts and advanced technologies to enhance mechanistic understanding.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This review does not yet provide actionable clinical insights for routine psychiatric care. It underscores the need for further research to validate findings and translate epigenetic signals into therapeutic targets. Clinicians should remain cautious about overinterpreting these preliminary results.

item.title: [7] A Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial of Intramuscular Olanzapine Versus Haloperidol for Acute Agitation in Hospitalized Adult Women With Bipolar I Disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study is a single-center, double-blind randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing intramuscular (IM) olanzapine (10 mg) versus haloperidol (5 mg) for acute agitation in 40 hospitalized adult women with bipolar I disorder during a manic episode. The primary outcome was agitation reduction measured by the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS), with secondary outcomes including the PANSS-Excited Component (PANSS-EC) and Modified Simpson-Angus Scale (MSAS).
FINDINGS: All 40 participants completed follow-up. RASS scores changed over time (p = 0.030), but there was no significant group-by-time interaction (p = 0.777) or overall group effect (p = 0.880). PANSS-EC showed a lower overall mean score in the olanzapine group (p = 0.043), though individual time-point comparisons and interaction effects were not significant. MSAS scores were low in the olanzapine group and zero in the haloperidol group. One participant in the haloperidol group experienced excessive sedation; no other adverse events were reported.
INTERPRETATION: The lack of significant differences in RASS trajectories and non-significant interaction effects for both RASS and PANSS-EC suggests no clear superiority of IM olanzapine over haloperidol for agitation in this population. The exploratory finding of lower PANSS-EC scores with olanzapine is not robust enough to conclude clinical benefit. The small sample size (n=40), absence of pretreatment scores, and single-center design limit generalizability and internal validity. Larger, multi-center RCTs with standardized baseline measurements are needed to confirm these preliminary findings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support a clear preference for IM olanzapine over haloperidol for acute agitation in hospitalized women with bipolar I disorder. Clinicians should continue to tailor treatment based on individual patient profiles, adverse effect profiles, and local guidelines until more definitive data emerge.

item.title: [7] Mobile Apps Supporting Medication Adherence in Substance Use Disorder Treatment: Narrative Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The review asks whether smartphone apps can support medication adherence in people with substance use disorders (SUDs), a population where poor adherence undermines effective pharmacotherapy. It synthesizes 22 studies describing app features and early evaluations, but was not designed to quantify clinical effectiveness.
FINDINGS: Seven feature types were identified: reminders/reinforcers (64% of apps), self-monitoring/goal tracking (64%), patient–provider communication (59%), information, community boards, external tracking, and gamification. Most studies were small feasibility or acceptability trials with self-reported outcomes and incomplete data; efficacy was rarely the primary endpoint. Usability ratings and engagement were consistently positive.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and heterogeneous, with high risk of bias from small, homogeneous samples and reliance on self-report. While user engagement and perceived usefulness are encouraging, there is no reliable evidence that any specific app feature improves medication adherence or clinical outcomes. Funding sources were not reported, so industry influence cannot be excluded.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, apps may be considered as adjuncts to support engagement, but they cannot be recommended as evidence-based adherence tools. Clinicians should monitor for data completeness and validate self-reported adherence with objective measures when possible.

item.title: [31] A Narrative Review of Myths and Misconceptions About Methylphenidate in the Treatment of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines persistent myths and misconceptions about methylphenidate (MPH) in ADHD treatment, aiming to counter treatment hesitancy and suboptimal prescribing. It synthesizes evidence from systematic reviews, meta-analyses, trials, pharmacokinetic studies, and guidelines across the lifespan.
FINDINGS: Twelve common misconceptions were identified, including concerns about insomnia, anxiety, growth suppression, abuse potential, and limited efficacy beyond childhood. Evidence from high-quality sources (e.g., RCTs, pharmacokinetic studies) refuted these myths, supporting MPH’s efficacy, tolerability, and formulation diversity (e.g., delayed-release/extended-release options).
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this study lacks systematic methodology (e.g., predefined search criteria, risk-of-bias assessment), relying instead on expert input and selective literature. While the counterarguments are evidence-based, the strength of conclusions depends on the quality and representativeness of cited sources. The review highlights gaps in clinician education but does not quantify the prevalence of these myths or their impact on prescribing.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should be aware of these myths and use evidence-based discussions with patients/families to improve adherence. However, this review does not provide new clinical data—its value lies in addressing misinformation rather than changing practice.

item.title: [24] Enhanced cognitive behavioural therapy for suicidality among people with comorbid mental and physical health conditions: study protocol of a pragmatic randomised controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The trial addresses whether an enhanced cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) added to standard care reduces suicidal ideation in adults with comorbid mental and physical health conditions. It is a pragmatic RCT (protocol only) designed to fill the evidence gap on psychotherapeutic interventions tailored to this high-risk group.
FINDINGS: The study will randomise participants to enhanced CBT plus standard care versus standard care alone, with primary outcome being post-intervention suicidal ideation severity. Secondary outcomes include self-harm, depression, anxiety, coping, hopelessness, impact of comorbidities, and mental well-being. Biomarker data (inflammation, HPA-axis, neural plasticity, tryptophan-kynurenine) will also be collected. Follow-up is planned at post-intervention and 3 months.
INTERPRETATION: As a protocol, no results are available; therefore, no effect sizes, confidence intervals, or p-values can be reported. The pragmatic design enhances external validity for routine psychiatric care, but the absence of published outcomes precludes any assessment of internal validity or clinical significance. The biomarker component is exploratory and may not directly inform immediate practice.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study could eventually inform whether enhanced CBT should be routinely offered to patients with comorbid mental and physical conditions who are suicidal, but results are not yet available. Clinicians should continue to follow current guidelines for managing suicidality while awaiting trial outcomes.

item.title: [20] Effectiveness of intervention using artificial intelligence for students with disabilities: systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether artificial intelligence (AI)-based interventions improve outcomes for students with disabilities, addressing concerns about model bias and ecological validity in special education. Sixteen studies were included, with only one randomized controlled trial (RCT).
FINDINGS: The overall effect size was large (Hedges' g = 1.263), with 87.5% of studies (14/16) reporting significant effects. Subgroup analyses showed the largest effects for cognitive outcomes, ADHD, university students, and when interventions were implemented by researchers. Only 12.5% of studies (2/16) reported non-significant results.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak due to the dominance of non-randomized designs (15/16 studies), small sample sizes, and high heterogeneity across disability types and outcomes. The large pooled effect size may be inflated by selection bias, lack of blinding, and publication bias. The single RCT limits causal inference, and subgroup findings are exploratory. Ethical concerns about AI bias and ecological validity remain unaddressed by the included studies.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support routine adoption of AI interventions in special education. Clinicians should remain cautious about overestimating benefits until higher-quality trials with clinically meaningful outcomes and long-term follow-up are conducted.

item.title: [19] Body and Movement Based Interventions in Psychotic Disorders: A Scoping Review of Treatments and Outcomes.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The review asks whether body and movement-based interventions (physical exercise, body–mind practices, dance) improve psychotic symptoms or motor outcomes in people with psychotic disorders, and how the field’s evidence base is structured. It is a scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) of 80 heterogeneous studies identified up to April 2025.
FINDINGS: Eighty studies were included; three intervention families emerged (physical exercise n≈30, body–mind n≈25, dance n≈25). Reported effects on psychosis symptoms ranged from no change to large improvements; motor outcomes were similarly mixed. Study designs, session counts (1–156), delivery formats (individual vs group), and providers varied widely; follow-up was often absent or short.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and heterogeneous, precluding firm conclusions. The review’s strength is its systematic mapping of intervention characteristics and outcomes, but the lack of standardized protocols, blinding, and control comparators limits internal validity. External validity is uncertain given the diversity of populations and settings. The field needs RCTs with clear mechanistic hypotheses and standardized outcome measures.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, no intervention can be recommended as an evidence-based adjunct for psychosis; clinicians should view these approaches as experimental while awaiting higher-quality trials.

item.title: [16] The efficacy of ketogenic interventions on neuropsychological & metabolic outcomes in serious mental illness & neurocognitive disorders: a systematic review & meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether ketogenic interventions (e.g., ketogenic diet, ketone supplements) improve neuropsychological and metabolic outcomes in individuals with serious mental illness (SMI) or neurocognitive disorders. The review synthesized evidence from case reports, single-arm trials, and controlled studies to assess efficacy and safety.
FINDINGS: Seventy-three studies were included (31 in SMI; 42 in neurocognitive disorders). In neurocognitive disorders, ketogenic interventions modestly improved cognitive performance (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.24, 95% CI [0.06, 0.43], p = 0.01, n = 587, k = 14, I² = 61%) and reduced body weight (mean difference [MD] -3.13 kg, 95% CI [-5.91, -0.35], p = 0.03, n = 80, k = 3, I² = 6%). In SMI, evidence was largely limited to case reports and single-arm trials, with anecdotal reports of symptom remission and mood improvements. Gastrointestinal symptoms were the most common adverse event.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence for neurocognitive disorders is more robust, with controlled trials showing modest but statistically significant cognitive and metabolic benefits. However, heterogeneity (I² = 61%) and small effect sizes suggest limited clinical significance. For SMI, the evidence is preliminary, consisting mostly of uncontrolled designs, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about efficacy or safety. High-quality randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are needed to confirm these findings and assess long-term outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Ketogenic interventions may offer modest cognitive and metabolic benefits in neurocognitive disorders, but the clinical impact is uncertain. For SMI, current evidence is insufficient to recommend ketogenic interventions in routine care. Clinicians should be cautious about potential gastrointestinal side effects and await further RCTs before considering these interventions.

item.title: [14] Mitochondrial Bioenergetics in Schizophrenia: a Systematic Review, Meta-analysis, and GRADE-Based Certainty Assessment.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This PRISMA-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis (through Dec 2025) assessed mitochondrial bioenergetics in schizophrenia across 47 human and animal studies, quantifying functional outcomes and biomarker changes while grading certainty with GRADE.
FINDINGS: Human studies showed reduced ATP-linked respiration (effect size not reported; high heterogeneity, I² > 90%). Complex III and IV activities were lower in schizophrenia, but Complex II (nuclear-encoded) showed no difference. Animal data mirrored trends but were imprecise. Overall certainty of evidence was rated "very low" due to bias, inconsistency, imprecision, and indirectness.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak despite many studies. High heterogeneity, unstable pooled estimates, and risk of bias (ROBINS-E/ROBINS-I, Newcastle-Ottawa) undermine confidence in the magnitude or specificity of mitochondrial dysfunction. Findings are preliminary; replication in rigorously designed, standardized studies is needed before clinical implications can be considered.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current results do not support changes to assessment or treatment of schizophrenia based on mitochondrial biomarkers. Clinicians should await higher-quality evidence before considering mitochondrial-targeted interventions.

item.title: [10] Art therapy for core symptoms in schizophrenia: An umbrella review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This umbrella review synthesised systematic reviews (SRs) on art therapy (music, dance, drama, horticultural, visual arts, multimodal) for core symptoms of schizophrenia, restricting evidence to randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and assessing methodological quality and outcome certainty.
FINDINGS: Thirteen SRs were included; 11 rated low or critically low on AMSTAR 2. Across 28 effect estimates, none had high GRADE certainty (3 moderate, 16 low, 9 very low). Negative-symptom estimates generally favoured art therapy, but were sensitive to blinding and publication bias; positive-symptom findings were inconclusive. Only one SR addressed cognitive outcomes.
INTERPRETATION: Confidence in the evidence is very low due to critically low-quality SRs, overlapping primary studies, and reliance on unblinded outcomes. While negative-symptom signals exist, they are fragile and not clinically definitive. High-quality, prospectively registered RCTs with blinded assessments are needed before firm conclusions can be drawn.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify changing practice; art therapy may be considered as an adjunct only with informed consent about uncertain benefits, pending better trials.

item.title: [9] When regulation disrupts treatment: controlled-substance policies, continuity of chronic disease care, and health equity.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This qualitative study embedded within the MINDSET 2.0 epilepsy RCT explores how controlled-substance policies create barriers to medication access and continuity of care, using patient-reported experiences from 53 adults with epilepsy in Arizona and Texas.
FINDINGS: Participants reported multiple interacting barriers (refill timing restrictions, pharmacy verification requirements, partial fills, insurance limits, prescriber-pharmacy coordination issues, travel/transportation) that disrupted routines, caused stress, and led to missed doses. One reported breakthrough seizures after a pharmacy stock delay; another considered stopping medication due to repeated refill difficulties. A 2026 clinician survey (n=236) corroborated high rates of refill difficulty (99%) and breakthrough seizures (96%) linked to missed doses.
INTERPRETATION: The study highlights credible, patient-centered evidence of cumulative access burdens from overlapping regulatory, payer, pharmacy, and supply factors. Strengths include thematic saturation and convergent clinician survey data, but limitations include small, epilepsy-specific sample and qualitative design (no effect sizes or controls). The clinical significance lies in the potential for disproportionate harm from rigid policies, though generalizability to other conditions or settings is uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should anticipate and mitigate controlled-substance access barriers (e.g., early refills, streamlined workflows) to prevent treatment interruptions, especially in patients with epilepsy or other chronic conditions requiring strict adherence.

item.title: [7] Implication of the ADCY1 Gene in Lithium Response in Bipolar Disorder by Genome-Wide Association Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This genome-wide association study (GWAS) meta-analysis examined whether genetic variation influences lithium response in 1,259 adults with bipolar disorder (BD) treated with lithium, combining new cases with two prior GWAS datasets to identify loci linked to treatment efficacy.
FINDINGS: A single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP), rs116927879 (A/G), reached genome-wide significance (p = 4.509 × 10⁻⁸) and mapped to the ADCY1 gene on chromosome 7. The SNP showed a consistent effect across all cohorts. Estimated SNP heritability for good lithium response was 20.3% (subjective response) and 15.6% (objective response). No significant genetic correlation was found with schizophrenia or major depressive disorder, and polygenic risk score analyses were negative. A weak sex interaction suggested males may be more likely to respond well.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is suggestive but preliminary. The study benefits from a relatively large sample and replication across cohorts, but the effect size at the genome-wide level is modest and the functional link to ADCY1 remains inferential (via splicing QTLs). The lack of replication with other psychiatric traits and the absence of clinical covariates (e.g., adherence, dosing) limit interpretability. The heritability estimates are moderate but do not yet translate into actionable biomarkers.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, this finding does not change practice. Lithium remains a first-line mood stabilizer in BD, and genotyping for rs116927879 is not recommended. Future studies must validate the association in diverse populations and clarify the biological mechanism before any clinical application can be considered.

item.title: [7] Association between distinct subgroups of perinatal depressive symptoms and exclusive breastfeeding behaviors: A prospective cohort study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This prospective cohort study in Hunan, China (n=304) examined whether different patterns of perinatal depressive symptoms (antenatal, postpartum, persistent, or none) differentially affect exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) behaviors, addressing prior inconsistencies by using repeated assessments across seven time points.
FINDINGS: After adjusting for confounders, women with persistent depressive symptoms were significantly less likely to practice EBF than those with no depressive symptoms (p < .05). No significant associations were found for antenatal or postpartum depressive symptom subgroups alone.
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests that persistent perinatal depressive symptoms may reduce EBF rates, while isolated antenatal or postpartum symptoms do not show the same association. However, as a single observational cohort from one tertiary hospital in China, generalisability is limited and causality cannot be inferred. The use of self-reported depression scales and WHO-defined EBF criteria may introduce measurement bias.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine repeated screening for depressive symptoms throughout the perinatal period may help identify women at risk for breastfeeding difficulties, but this finding should be confirmed in larger, more diverse cohorts before changing practice.

item.title: [7] Recognition and management of semaglutide overdose and intoxi​cation: a narrative review for clinicians.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: With rising use of the GLP-1 receptor agonist semaglutide, clinicians are encountering more overdoses. This narrative review synthesises human data on semaglutide pharmacology and excessive exposures to guide recognition and management.
FINDINGS: The overdose syndrome is dominated by prolonged gastrointestinal toxicity (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, anorexia) lasting days to weeks due to a ~1-week elimination half-life. Serious outcomes arise from volume depletion, electrolyte disturbances and acute kidney injury; hypoglycaemia is uncommon in isolated overdose but can occur with co-ingestants or falsified products. Evidence is drawn from case reports/series and pharmacovigilance analyses; no controlled trials of overdose management exist.
INTERPRETATION: The review is transparent about the low certainty of evidence: recommendations rest largely on case-level data and pharmacological reasoning. Strengths include a practical toxidrome description and clear triage priorities; limitations include lack of quantitative incidence estimates and absence of comparative data. The clinical effect size is uncertain, but the mechanistic rationale for supportive care is strong.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For now, management should focus on aggressive antiemesis, fluid/electrolyte resuscitation and glucose monitoring, with airway protection and prolonged observation. Systems-level prevention (device design, dispensing standards, patient education) may be more impactful than acute interventions.

item.title: [7] Associations of meeting the guidelines for 24-hour movement behaviors with depressive symptoms and perceived stress across the first postpartum year.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This secondary analysis of the Postpartum 24/7 cohort study (n=50) examined whether adherence to 24-hour movement behavior guidelines (physical activity, sedentary behavior, sleep) during the first postpartum year was associated with lower depressive symptoms and perceived stress, using device-based and self-reported measures.
FINDINGS: Sleep quality guideline adherence was linked to lower depressive symptoms (β = -2.44, p=0.002) and perceived stress (β = -3.87, p<0.001), while avoiding pre-bed screen time reduced perceived stress (β = -2.43, p=0.041). Meeting more guidelines cumulatively was associated with lower depressive symptoms (β = -0.81, p=0.02) and stress (β = -1.90, p<0.001). Sleep duration and efficiency improved over time (p=0.043 and p=0.017, respectively), but physical activity and sedentary behavior guideline adherence showed no independent association with outcomes after adjustment.
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests sleep quality and screen-time avoidance may benefit postpartum mental health, with additive effects when multiple 24-hour movement guidelines are met. However, the very small sample (n=50), single-site design, and secondary analysis nature limit generalizability and causal inference. The associations are statistically significant but effect sizes are modest (e.g., β=-2.44 for depressive symptoms), and clinical significance remains uncertain. Larger, prospective studies with diverse populations are needed to confirm these findings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence is too preliminary to change practice, but highlights sleep hygiene and screen-time reduction as potential targets for postpartum mental health support. Clinicians should monitor sleep quality and screen habits in postpartum patients while awaiting more robust data.

item.title: [7] Ketamine promotes strategic and efficient approach-avoidance conflict resolution.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study tested whether a single dose of intranasal ketamine (50 mg) improves strategic decision-making in a controlled approach-avoidance conflict task compared with placebo and oral lorazepam (1 mg) in a randomized crossover trial of 34 healthy volunteers.
FINDINGS: All 34 participants completed all three conditions. Ketamine increased net token gains by 57% versus control (β = 0.09, 95% CI 0.05–0.13; p < 0.001) and by 33% versus lorazepam (β = 0.05, 95% CI 0.01–0.09; p = 0.009). Behavior under ketamine was more strongly driven by outcome value than threat probability, and response latencies for approach and withdrawal were faster. Lorazepam produced a less selective increase in approach behavior.
INTERPRETATION: The randomized crossover design with blinding of behavioral assessors strengthens internal validity, but the sample consisted of healthy, medication-free adults, limiting generalizability to clinical populations. The effect sizes are statistically significant yet modest in absolute terms; their clinical relevance for routine psychiatric care remains uncertain. The absence of adverse events is reassuring but short-term follow-up precludes safety conclusions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These preliminary findings suggest ketamine may acutely enhance value-based decision-making, but translation to patient care cannot be assumed; further trials in clinical populations with longer follow-up are needed before any bedside change is warranted.

item.title: [6] Distinct therapeutic roles of diet control and exercise in metabolic disorder-related depression: insights from metabolic and gut microbiota signatures.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This preclinical study in mice investigated whether non-pharmacological interventions (diet change or exercise) could reverse metabolic disorder-related depression-like behaviors induced by a high-fat diet (HFD), focusing on hippocampal glutamate transporter expression, circuit hyperactivity, and gut microbiota signatures.
FINDINGS: Switching from HFD to normal chow at week 9 ameliorated most metabolic abnormalities and anhedonia but did not restore insulin sensitivity or behavioral despair. Mild treadmill exercise prevented further weight gain but did not improve metabolic dysfunction or depression-like behaviors. Neither intervention restored ventral hippocampal glutamate transporter expression, astrocytic integrity, or ventral hippocampus–nucleus accumbens circuit hyperactivity. Behavioral despair correlated strongly with systemic insulin resistance (not overweight or corticosterone), and a distinct gut microbiota signature was linked to depressive behaviors and astrocytic dysfunction.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides mechanistic insights in a controlled mouse model, suggesting that insulin resistance—not obesity per se—may drive this depression subtype. However, the interventions tested did not reverse the core neural or behavioral pathology, indicating limited translational potential at this stage. The gut microbiota findings are exploratory and require validation. The lack of behavioral improvement despite metabolic changes underscores the complexity of metabolic-psychiatric comorbidity.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not support immediate changes to clinical practice for metabolic disorder-related depression. They highlight insulin resistance as a potential biomarker but do not demonstrate that diet or mild exercise alone can reverse depression-like behaviors in this model. Further translational research is needed before any bedside implications can be considered.

item.title: [6] Anticholinergic Medications and Health in Adults with Autism or Intellectual Disability.
item.description:
