BACKGROUND: This retrospective cohort study examined whether exposure to anticholinergic (AC) medications is associated with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD), falls, and mortality in middle-aged and older adults with autism, intellectual disability (ID), or both, compared to controls. The study used US Medicare/Medicaid claims data from 2017–2019.
FINDINGS: AC medication exposure was substantially higher in all clinical groups (autism+ID: 92.5%, ID-only: 88.6%, autism-only: 80.0%) than in controls (61.3%). Exposure was associated with increased risks of ADRD, falls, and mortality across groups, with stronger associations observed in autism and/or ID populations. Associations showed stepwise increases with higher AC potency levels. Sensitivity analyses excluding antidepressant/antipsychotic users yielded similar trends.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s large sample and validated algorithms strengthen internal validity, but the retrospective design and reliance on claims data limit causal inference. Confounding by indication (e.g., underlying conditions requiring AC drugs) remains a concern, though sensitivity analyses partially addressed this. The magnitude of associations appears clinically relevant, particularly in high-exposure groups, but effect sizes are not quantified in the abstract. External validity is constrained by the US Medicare/Medicaid population, which may not generalize to other healthcare systems.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest AC medication exposure may be a modifiable risk factor for adverse aging outcomes in autistic adults and those with ID. Clinicians should review AC burden in these patients, particularly when prescribing, and consider deprescribing where appropriate—while balancing psychiatric stability. Further prospective studies are needed to confirm causality and quantify risk.

item.title: [26] A Systematic Review of Randomized Clinical Trials Evaluating Adapted Psychological Interventions for Depression in Black and Latino Populations in the United States.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The review asks whether culturally adapted psychological therapies reduce depressive symptoms in Black and Latino adults in the US, where depression is common and often undertreated. It synthesizes randomized trials published up to July 2025.
FINDINGS: Nine RCTs (seven in Latinos, two in Blacks) were included. Most interventions combined cultural tailoring with collaborative care. At 1–3 months the pooled standardized mean difference (SMD) was –0.28 (95 % CI not reported, P = .02); at 4–6 months SMD was –0.33 (P < .00001). Subgroup analyses found no significant differences by delivery format or type of adaptation.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is small (nine trials, modest sample sizes) and heterogeneous in design, limiting precision and the ability to detect which adaptation features matter. The statistically significant effects are small (SMD ≈ –0.3), suggesting modest clinical benefit on average. Risk of bias and publication bias were not assessed in the abstract, so confidence in the magnitude of effect is low.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Culturally adapted therapies appear to produce small improvements in depressive symptoms in these populations, but the paucity and heterogeneity of trials preclude firm recommendations on optimal adaptation strategies; routine adoption should be cautious pending larger, well-controlled studies.

item.title: [25] Effects of specialised and centralised versus generalised and decentralised outpatient treatment for progressed bipolar disorder: Results from the CAG Bipolar randomised controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study tested whether specialized, centralized outpatient care (CAG Bipolar) improves outcomes versus decentralized, general psychiatric care for patients with advanced bipolar disorder in a pragmatic RCT (n=1,134).
FINDINGS: Over 12 months, there was no difference in number (RR 0.94, 95 % CI 0.74–1.14, p=0.6) or duration (0.16 days, 95 % CI –4.10–4.42, p=0.9) of psychiatric hospitalizations. Lithium (RR 1.19, 95 % CI 1.05–1.33) and antipsychotics—especially quetiapine (RR 1.17, 95 % CI 1.03–1.30)—were prescribed more in CAG Bipolar, and patient satisfaction with care was higher. No group differences were seen for coercion, depressive or manic symptoms, quality of life, or perceived stress.
INTERPRETATION: The trial is large and pragmatic, suggesting that centralizing care does not reduce hospital use or symptom burden in advanced bipolar disorder. Higher guideline-concordant prescribing and satisfaction likely reflect better access to specialized expertise, but the lack of change in core clinical outcomes and the open-label design limit conclusions about causality. Uncertainty remains about long-term effects and whether increased medication translates into better functional outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For patients with progressed bipolar disorder, switching to a specialized centralized outpatient unit may improve satisfaction and medication choices without reducing hospitalizations or symptoms; thus, shared decision-making about referral should weigh these trade-offs.

item.title: [17] The American Society of Clinical Psychopharmacology Task Force Consensus Statement on Combination Psychopharmacology.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The American Society of Clinical Psychopharmacology (ASCP) Task Force developed a consensus statement to guide rational combination psychopharmacology in psychiatry, addressing the lack of empirical evidence for polydrug regimens. The expert panel (60 psychiatrists and pharmacists from 16 countries) used a two-round Delphi survey to reach consensus on 66 items, with ≥75% agreement required for inclusion.
FINDINGS: Consensus (≥75% agreement) was achieved on 62/66 items (94%). Key principles included reserving combination therapy for complex, treatment-resistant cases, favoring nonredundant drug mechanisms, avoiding nonclozapine antipsychotic combinations, and prioritizing shared decision-making. Before augmentation, the panel recommended ensuring optimized dosing, adherence, and diagnostic accuracy. Switching was favored over augmenting after minimal improvement.
INTERPRETATION: This is a consensus statement based on expert opinion, not empirical data, with high internal consistency (94% consensus) but no direct evidence of efficacy or safety. Strengths include global expert input and structured methodology (Delphi process). Limitations include lack of patient outcomes, no systematic literature review, and potential bias from unblinded expert opinions. The recommendations are pragmatic but preliminary, highlighting gaps in evidence rather than proven practices.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These principles may guide clinicians in rational polypharmacy, particularly for treatment-resistant cases, but should be applied cautiously. The statement underscores the need for more research on combination psychopharmacology efficacy and safety. Clinicians should prioritize monotherapy optimization and shared decision-making before resorting to complex regimens.

item.title: [15] Psychedelics and Sleep: Preclinical and Human Studies-A Systematic Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review (PRISMA-guided) examined how classic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, DMT/ayahuasca) affect sleep architecture and quality in preclinical and human studies, motivated by psychedelics’ rapid-acting antidepressant potential and sleep’s role in emotional regulation.
FINDINGS: Preclinical studies consistently showed acute REM sleep suppression, delayed REM onset, increased wakefulness, and transient non-REM disruption. Human data were heterogeneous: randomized trials found prolonged REM latency after psilocybin and reduced REM duration after ayahuasca; SWA effects were mixed (ayahuasca increased early-cycle SWA, psilocybin reduced delta power). Subjective sleep quality showed little acute change in controlled settings, though one large naturalistic study reported reduced sleep disturbances after psilocybin. Bedtime dosing was more disruptive than daytime dosing.
INTERPRETATION: Evidence quality was fair-to-poor with notable risk of bias; preclinical findings are robust but human studies are limited and inconsistent. The clinical significance of these sleep changes remains unclear, and no causal link to therapeutic effects has been established. Larger, well-controlled polysomnographic studies are needed to determine whether psychedelic-induced sleep modulation is clinically meaningful.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support altering dosing times or sleep expectations in routine practice; clinicians should remain cautious about bedtime use due to potential acute disruption, but no practice changes are warranted based on these findings alone.
